Raitenhaslach
RITE-un-hahss-lahkh
n. (the Bavarian Cistercian abbey of 1146 on the Salzach, below Burghausen)
From Old High German hasal, hazel, with a personal name; the hazel wood of Raito.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Raitenhaslach stands on the Salzach below Burghausen and was founded in 1146 from Salem, the first Cistercian house in what is now Upper Bavaria. It grew rich on the salt trade of the river, holding salt rights at Reichenhall and shipping down the Salzach and the Inn, and it founded daughters at Fuerstenzell and elsewhere. The church was rebuilt in baroque between 1694 and 1739 with frescoes by Johann Zick; the abbey was dissolved in 1803 and the buildings now serve the Technical University of Munich. This dictionary records Raitenhaslach for the salt, which Scripture uses with unusual precision. Christ makes his people salt and then names the one failure that matters, “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Mat 5:13). Speech is to be seasoned the same way, “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6). Salt was required on every offering as a covenant sign, “neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking” (Lev 2:13), and a covenant of salt is the figure for one that does not spoil, “it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines salt as a substance used for seasoning and preserving; savour as taste or odour; to season as to give a relish to; a covenant as a mutual agreement; and preservation as the act of keeping from decay.

expand to see more

SALT, n. Common salt is the muriate of soda, a substance used for seasoning certain kinds of food, and for the preservation of meat.

SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste or smell; relish; also, flavor.

SEASON, v.t. To render palatable, or to give a higher relish to, by the addition of salt, spices or condiments.

COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; a stipulation.

PRESERVATION, n. The act of preserving or keeping safe; the act of keeping from injury, destruction or decay.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:13 — "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men."

Col 4:6 — "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man."

Lev 2:13 — "And every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt; neither shalt thou suffer the salt of the covenant of thy God to be lacking from thy meat offering: with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt."

Num 18:19 — "All the heave offerings of the holy things, which the children of Israel offer unto the LORD, have I given thee, and thy sons and thy daughters with thee, by a statute for ever: it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD unto thee and to thy seed with thee."

Modern Corruption

Bavarian abbey of 1146 on the Salzach: the first Cistercian house in Upper Bavaria, grown rich on the salt trade of its own river.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salt is defined by what it does to something else. It is useless in a heap and essential in a dish, which is exactly how Christ deploys the figure for his people, “Ye are the salt of the earth” (Mat 5:13), with the one failure named immediately, “if the salt have lost his savour” (Mat 5:13). A monastery that shipped salt down a river should have found the sermon easy.

The second use is covenantal and is easy to miss. Salt had to be on every offering, as a standing sign that the covenant would not spoil, “every oblation of thy meat offering shalt thou season with salt” (Lev 2:13), and the arrangement with the priests is described in the same terms, “it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19). Speech gets the same treatment, seasoned rather than bland or corrosive, “that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man” (Col 4:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek halas (G217), salt; Greek moraino (G3471), to become tasteless; Hebrew melach (H4417), salt; Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant; Greek artuo (G741), to season.

expand to see more

Greek halas (G217) — salt, the people's own figure; “Ye are the salt of the earth”, Matthew 5:13.

Greek moraino (G3471) — to make foolish, to lose savour; “if the salt have lost his savour”, Matthew 5:13.

Greek artuo (G741) — to season, of speech; “seasoned with salt”, Colossians 4:6.

Hebrew melach (H4417) — salt, required on every offering; “shalt thou season with salt”, Leviticus 2:13.

Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, here one of salt; “it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD”, Numbers 18:19.

Usage

"“Ye are the salt of the earth” (Mat 5:13) — useless in a heap, essential in a dish."

"“seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6) — speech neither bland nor corrosive."

"“it is a covenant of salt for ever before the LORD” (Num 18:19) — a bond that does not spoil."
